title: Not alone in it
hookLine: Christians see in the cross a God who suffers with humanity
last: NOT AS I WILL, BUT AS THOU WILT.

cards: The garden prayer asked for the cup to pass. In Matthew's telling, it doesn't. Within hours there is an arrest, a trial before the high priest, a night of denials, and then a place called Golgotha.

Christian teaching reads the cross in more than one way: some readings ask what it paid for, or what it won. Today's asks something quieter. Who is on that cross, and which side of the pain is he standing on?
Watching it from above, or inside it?

teach.b: First, a name. In its first chapter, Matthew's Gospel gives a child the name Emmanuel, and translates it for its readers: "God with us." Not above us, not watching us.
With. Second, the cross. Christians read the crucifixion through that name.

teach.h: INSIDE THE PAIN, NOT WATCHING IT.
teach.b: In their telling, the one hanging there is no stranger to pain, watching from far off. He is inside it: betrayed by a friend, deserted, beaten, mocked.

Near the end, Matthew records him crying out the opening line of a psalm: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" That's the King James wording. Even feeling abandoned, in this reading, is a place he has been.
The Letter to the Hebrews says: "For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities." A double negative, almost shy. It means he can be touched.
He knows weakness from the inside.
Fourth, how churches say it. Some theologians speak of God himself suffering on the cross. Others hold that the divine nature cannot suffer, and that the Son suffered truly in his human nature.
Both keep hold of the same thing: on the cross, Christians say, God came into the worst of human pain, not only above it. The cup is not taken away.
In this reading, it is drunk by someone inside suffering, so that nobody in it is alone.

how: Christians meditate on the cross, especially in Holy Week and on Good Friday, as the place where God shares human suffering, and visit the sick and grieving as a work of mercy.

o: a title meaning God the judge, high above us
a Hebrew word for the high priest's prayer
a name meaning God with us, inside the pain

games.q: what's inside the cross reading — tap the pairs.
p: touched with the feeling of our infirmities

s: Matthew's Gospel translates the name Emmanuel for its readers
all churches describe Christ's suffering in exactly the same words
some speak of God suffering; others say the Son suffered in his human nature.
Hebrews says Christ cannot be touched by human weakness
it says the opposite, with a double negative: he can.

games.q: you're reading Hebrews: "we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities." what is the double negative saying?
o: he is kept far from human weakness.
he can be touched; he knows weakness from the inside.
games.why: "not... cannot" means he can. Christians read it as a God who knows suffering from the inside, not from a distance.

practice: Picture someone who is suffering right now: a friend, a parent, a neighbor, someone in the news.
Breathing in, say their name silently; breathing out, say: not alone, and if the mind starts drafting advice, let the version go and come back to the name. If you pray, you can hold them in prayer.

wordCard.voice: Emmanuel, the name Matthew gives Jesus, meaning God with us, inside suffering and not only above it. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew, from Isaiah 7:14; Matthew 1:23 translates it: God with us.

carryVoice: Your line: he can be touched. No advice needed, only company. That's day seven hundred seventeen.
